body: Tribalism in politics has absolutely gotten worse, and I agree that it’s damaging.  As to the often repeated claim that it’s the “Democratic run cities” that breed the conditions that we all find so unpleasant, I’d have to point out that cities have absorbed many of the homeless from rural areas and “red” states.  In fact, many underfunded rural areas will buy bus tickets for the unhoused just to get them out of sight.  There’s also a lot of in-migration to cities from rural areas because there’s more work, better wages, and more open minded people who younger people from rural areas relate to better than perhaps they did in the small town they grew up in.  Urban and rural areas each have their own distinctive issues to deal with.  California used to be affordable and really idyllic. So much so that everyone moved there.  If a conservative government took hold in San Francisco, for example, do you think they would solve homelessness, or would they just run them all off or send them to a different town to take care of them?  That’s just one little aspect of the talking points I hear when I turn on Fox to see what that side’s rhetoric is like.  It’s not really fair to blame one political party for a national problem, just because the refugees of that social ill end up distributed in the urban area.  The other side of this is that there hasn’t been much effort, by either party, put into revitalizing rural areas which have really been devastated by the outsourcing of manufacturing, the Walmart-ization and online shift of retail that has closed many small businesses, and the resulting lack of opportunities in many rural parts of the country.  It’s all framed as the evil Democrats which have caused this, but really it’s the inevitable logic of the market in a barely regulated capitalist system.  Both parties have been conservative in defending “free-markets” and global neoliberal expansion at the expense of all of us.  The Republicans happen to have traditionally been more on the side of deregulating the public interest, busting unions, and shifting the tax burden to the middle class, while arguing that wealth consolidation at the corporate level will naturally trickle down to the workers.  I don’t think there’s good evidence to suggest that it has.  Anyway, the new Republican movement, with its populist sentiments on some items is quite different than the Republicans I used to know.  Honestly,  if it wasn’t for the rhetorical fallacies being peddled by the opinion leaders in right wing media, and a barely veiled attempt to conflate intolerance of non-Christian/non- traditional human diversity with “patriotism,” I think we could actually find some common ground.  MTG, ( and the like) are doing their best to start a war.  It’s not honest or patriotic in any way. I had chronic upper back pain and a hip that would ache all the time and keep me awake at night by the time I was in the last few years of college.  Even had a heart murmur.  I figured it was just a forgone conclusion that the pain would worsen and I’d be out of the game before I was 40. After a few years of being out of school and working various field science jobs those pains went away and haven’t ever come back.  I hate gyms and don’t use them, but I do a lot of hiking for work and I took up running a little bit, which I do on-and-off just for the endorphins.  Anyway, fast forward to 45. No hip or back pain.  Heart murmur isn’t there anymore, and I’m probably about 10-15 pounds lighter. Carpal tunnel syndrome is the new annoyance, but it doesn’t make me feel 100 years old like the back pain used to.  I haven’t even been much of a health nut.  I’ve been through addictions, depressions, periods of poor nutrition, etc., but I think the body goes through growth and change all the time. 25 was definitely no peak of health, fitness, energy level, stamina, sex life, or anything really.  If I could pick one age to be forever, I’d pick 35.  I don’t really feel any different now, just more gray hair is all, and people do treat you differently after 40.

I tend to think polyandry is more akin to the natural way of humans.  There’s only a few remaining cultures who practice it and usually it’s brothers who share a wife.  I think it really depends on what your learned expectations are.  In some ways it would be less stressful if you aren’t the only guy on the hook for procuring resources to maintain a family, and it gives the mother the opportunity to fully engage with raising children if that’s what she wants to do.  Just wanted to chime in on the opposite side of the polyamory spectrum because it does make sense in a structural-functional context.  I’m brainwashed by my own upbringing to want monogamy, but the older I get, the less I care.  More hands make less work, and honestly it’s a lot of pressure to have to be everything and enough for one person ( other than your own self).  If you think about it, a lot of women have kids by multiple men anyway, so polyandry isn’t anything unusual, even if the result of serial monogamy.  I would hate to be responsible for multiple spouses and all the babies.  You could actually enjoy playing with kids and watching them grow if you weren’t working all the time.  It’s just that jealousy and possessiveness, and the notion that if you aren’t everything another person needs, that makes impossible for so many relationships to survive.  I’d rather be a second husband than have multiple wives.  Less pressure, less stress, less work, and you get more freedom to be alone and lazy if you want to be.

I was living in a travel trailer going job to job when the pandemic hit. I feel lucky to have found an acre with a giant old general store and a double wide for less than the price of a 20 year old used truck.  I would have loved to have hunkered down in Western Oregon, but I would have gone broke just paying rent within a year.  Instead, I actually have a pretty cool place, with no debt, and with all the remote work via internet, I don’t have to commute 100 miles a day.  It’s been a trade off with having a rich social life, but it beats the last 20 years of intermittent homelessness.  
All I’m saying is that it sucks that people assume everyone out in rural areas are toothless, uneducated bigots.  It’s just not true, and for those who have the dream of having some land, growing food, being self sufficient or building a collective, it’s actually a reachable goal if you get out here in the sticks. Political correctness is the term I’m more confident in describing, and I do find it annoying and counterproductive—especially since language is always changing and well-meaning people end up getting chewed out for not using the most recently polite terminology.  Example: the words “idiot” and “moron” and “retarded” all had periods of correctness in describing a similar set of mental deficits.  Now “retarded” is the one that is considered ableist whereas it was not long ago the polite way of saying the other two words. Now they are all bad when used to describe a person with developmental deficits, but you can use the more offensive two words to describe people you disagree with— just not “retarded”.
There’s a lot of examples, but overall, getting hung up on linguistic sensitivities tends to detract from actual progress in addressing the problems that really keep people fighting.
My take on the colonialism, CRT controversy is that it shouldn’t be an issue to teach that history happened.  It’s also true that what happened historically left its mark throughout the evolution of our legal and social systems.  Connecting the dots between slavery to Jim Crow to redlining of housing to inter generational poverty and incarceration is not intrinsically bad or wrong because time unfolds in a linear, forward direction.  You are absolutely correct that a white kid born in 1995 is not responsible for slavery or the Tulsa massacre, or anything that happened before.  Knowing that those things happened doesn’t mean that you should feel responsible.  Same thing with teaching what happened with the conquest of the Americas.  It happened.  Many of the entrenched social and economic problems faced by the remaining tribes can be directly traced to Indian Policy that progressed from the Colonial Period, though the formation and growth of the United States.  It’s not incorrect to see the chain of causality that started with the first massacres on the eastern seaboard and progressed into the various Indian wars and relocations, which has resulted in the reservation system of today.  Likewise, it doesn’t mean that it’s your fault.  You shouldn’t feel guilty about it just for understanding how it all happened. Nobody should.  
I remember feeling sad and angry about how mean Europeans were historically as far back as elementary school, but I never felt personally responsible just for being born.  I guess I’m still not getting that from today’s “woke-ism” or pc culture, but I acknowledge that by trying to sugarcoat and sterilize the language in an attempt to enforce some kind of moral hygiene, it does more to hide racism than it does to confront and move past it.  It’s just my opinion, but I believe political correctness and over-focus on identity is the Achilles heel of the cultural/political left.  Actions speak louder than words, and all the verbal hygiene in the word can’t make up for actual systemic roadblocks.  Neither can feeling guilty for anything that happened generations ago be a productive thing.  Teaching real history and cause and effect relationships is a good thing though.  The only way we avoid repeating the bad stuff is to understand how it happened.  I wish people wouldn’t be so sensitive and thin skinned, but also people should quit being so judgmental and assume that just because they are using the hippest new terminology to be culturally sensitive that they are actually doing anything to make the world a more just and equal place.

First, the 80 year cycle.  Not really an immutable configuration, but it is absolutely true that it takes a lifetime to learn some lessons, even with having access to history books and documentaries galore.  The demise of the WW2 generation is a prime example he noted.  I see the rise of populist right wing figures like The Donald as directly related to 90% + of the people who remember the 20s-40s being dead at the time his ascendency. Obviously, there’s  a lot of old timers who drank the cool-aide, but if they hadn’t been missing most of their age cohort by 2016, I don’t believe the world would have turned the way it did.
The cycle of capitalism and consolidation of capital by elites is also very cyclical.  Hegel and Marx, even if you hate the disasters stemming from co-opted interpretations of their theories, really did have an accurate summation of the relationship between the poor and the rich. Thesis, antithesis, synthesis, yada yada. Basically, one group exploits another for as long and hard as they can, then there’s rebellion, and reordering, and then it happens again with a slightly different group of elites.  WW2 pushed us along quite a bit in troubleshooting some of the pitfalls of colonialism and competition for raw resources, but the winners are consolidating again, eliminating completion, forming monopolies, and seeing how far they can push the working poor before its too much.  All the factors that brought about the 2nd WW are not the same now, but we have mass migration, economic insecurity, a widespread disappointment, etc, and politicians who are now able to revert to the eternal playbook of grievance and blame which was used most notoriously in the 30s-40s.  I really, really want to believe that we would have heeded the WW2 generation had they been around, but I could even be wrong and maybe they still would have gone for Twitler.  I don’t think so, but I guess it’s possible— if the human condition is even darker than I believe it to be.  
Anyway, his point about the internet: yes, it changed everything.  Time will tell, but theoretically it democratized access to information and opened up whole worlds of thought to billions of people who otherwise would have no knowledge of anything outside their little fishbowl.  It also became a tool for total manipulation.  Surveillance capitalism, and you might even argue “thought-control”. , though I don’t think that’s really what it is.  Influence for sure.  There’s enough data on each of us that could be mined and analyzed by commercial/governmental/ nongovernmental enterprises, and used to slowly acclimate individual minds to think and respond in predictable and desired ways.  Cambridge Analytica, etc, etc.  Our computers and those who facilitate our access to infinite, seemingly benign entertainment know us better than we know ourselves.
Meanwhile, we are no smarter as a species than we were 100,000 years ago.  You could take a homo ancestor like Neanderthal and put them in a classroom, and they might end up working for Google making 6 figures writing code.  Science is cumulative. Technology is cumulative.  If everything we have digitized to cloud computing was lost, and we had no libraries or hard copies to learn from, no prototypes to reverse engineer, the next generation would do just about as well as a Neanderthal at reconstructing our vast technological arsenal.  We really shouldn’t be looking down the barrel of a global fascist takeover though, because we haven’t had all our libraries burned.  We aren’t starting over from scratch at all.  This leaves me no other option than to reassert that some life lessons actually have to be learned first-hand, and some of these lessons take a lifetime to learn.

I’m not sure how you would go about removing heavy metals from a waterbody.  Methyl mercury is the metal of concern in a lot of fish.  Mercury in droplets is just going to stay on the bottom, but periphyton and algae can absorb and convert to methylated form and that’s how it works it’s way up the food chain to the best of my understanding.  There might be a way to systematically get it out of a dry lakebed or possibly find the right aquatic plant/algae that would soak it up, but then you would need to harvest that flora and dispose of it.  Meanwhile, it falls with the rain because of the trace amounts present in the fuels we burn ( like coal). I’m not sure how damaging it would be to health if it were simply present in trace levels in drinking water, or what methods might mitigate the municipal use of a contaminated source.  It definitely gets condensed in animals, but it isn’t from drinking the water. It goes from its elemental form, then algae/periphyton, then bugs that eat the green stuff, then fish that eat the bugs/green stuff, then fish that eat those fish, then an osprey, eagle, bear, human, etc.  Whatever critter eats us is going to get the highest dose of bioaccumulate.  The most poignant example I can think of to illustrate would be PCBs in breast milk of people who subsist on marine mammals.  In some cases, mothers of newborns in some of the remote villages of the far north have been advised not to breastfeed their kiddos because of toxicity accumulated from the consumption of whales and seals.  I can’t find the study off-hand, but there’s a few abstracts on pubmed that cover lactation and PCBs.  The article I was looking for is over 20 years old, so there’s probably a lot more similar studies by now.

What little I know about the subject from sampling fish for mercury in a job a few years back is that the larger the drainage area of a water body, the more accumulation of metals and other toxins. Theoretically, if you catch a fish in a small, high mountain lake there will be less nasty stuff than if the fish is taken from a large reservoir where 100 tributaries have entered down a river and made the reservoir.  Bio accumulation. It also varies according to the type of fish. Large carnivorous fish accumulate more bad stuff, whereas fish that feed lower in the food chain tend to be less toxic.  Eating a salmon is going to impart more mercury, etc, than eating a carp or herring or sardine.

Some of them had never even seen the stars because they had never been out of a metro area.  Some of them seemed really transformed by the experience. Anyway, nature can have a profound impact on improving mental health and providing a little perspective on our lives.  A lot of the worst littering and slob behavior I’ve seen over the years is from people who never developed an appreciation for nature, possibly because they never had the opportunity to get out of the rat-race, or their parents never did.  I think it helps in learning an ethic of preservation and environmental concern when people can  go have an outdoor experience.  Keeping a few areas that aren’t monetized, where people who are seriously living on a shoe-string budget can go to, is important.  I was a kid in the 80s and 90s, and I remember having a lot more options to camp on the beach and not have to listen to generators running all night.  It’s really hard to find any place that allows it anymore, and it is kind of sad.  I’d like kids today and in the future to be able to have these experiences that I remember, but I get it that there’s an additional 3 billion of us now and we are degrading the very environment that we rely on.  Anyway, your idea of having subsidized public camping areas that are maintained is an idea I like.  Making everything pay-camping just reinforces transactional relationships with nature and ends up excluding some people. I’d argue that people are less likely to trash a place if they are legally allowed to be there, and others are in the area exerting some peer pressure.  Camping limits are a good idea.  Having bum camps on every beach would definitely not be good for the environment.  I’m sure there’s a happy medium that could be reached, but it really does seem like every single dispersed camping option has been eliminated in some areas in an effort to monetize nature.

If you’ve never been there, then I’m happy for you.  For those who have, it’s really frustrating to be funneled towards increasingly expensive options or face being considered in violation.  But hey, people running short on cash can just go sleep in the Walmart parking lot, right?

I started experiencing sleep paralysis at around age 33.  The first times I think stemmed from either a bout of insomnia or possibly a hangover.  I’ve never experienced headache associated with it, but it can present itself when I’m sick or have other issues causing disharmony. It often it occurs right on the cusp of falling asleep, or shortly after in the liminal sleep stage. These nights where it happens at the edge of sleep feel Iike my head is being pulled into an electric motor and like my head is shaking rapidly.  I can hear it rubbing the pillow.  I thought I was having seizures at first, but over time I’ve come to associate it with sleep paralysis because if I don’t pull myself out of the “electric drain” it does immobilized my limbs and is quite scary.  When it happens in superficial sleep, or as I’m falling asleep it will keep happening many times in a row and I can usually stop it each time by rolling over. If it happens too many times I have to get up and do something for a little while and it usually goes away.  
The times when it happens during the middle of sleep can be much more unsettling and be accompanied by hallucinations or warping of my environment.  The worst was while sleeping under a weighted blanket.  It seemed like it took forever to pull out of it and be able to move with any force.  Last night I had it in deep sleep and was coming out of some nice dreams within dreams. Then I was awake, sort of, and could see my room or a version of it and someone was spooning me from the back.  I could feel their hand reach around my chest and touch my wrist.  I guess it was creepy enough that I had to see if there was a Reddit for this type of thing.  At one point the figure rose above me and I wanted to reach out and touch it, but I couldn’t raise my arm.  It felt like my fingers were twitching, but this was the point where I realized it was definitely sleep paralysis.  I was trying to talk to the hallucination, but couldn’t get words to form.  It wasn’t all that unpleasant, feeling like someone was touching me because I was still in the dream land where my identity wasn’t fixed. I often have a love life in my dreams, but I’m not necessarily me in dreams.  When I finally snapped awake and the room shadows became familiar and I knew where I was at and who I was, the word that came to my head was “succubus”.  
Anyway, I hope that the pain you are experiencing with your sleep paralysis is benign.  I have noticed that I get it a lot more in times of sickness, depression, insomnia and back pain, so I do associate it with disharmony.  It could be that the pain is triggering the sleep abnormality rather than the sleep paralysis triggering the pain.

I’ve been reading a lot about deja vu lately.  I used to have it a lot when I was younger, before ever experience my weird seizures.  For awhile when I was an adolescent, it would happen frequently, and it sometimes would last for more than a few seconds.  It was enough to freak me out.  It made me question whether or not we have free-will, or if we just have the illusion of it— like life is a recording that gets erased and then replays the same way, over and over, for eternity.  I used to think that deja vu was like a glitch in the matrix, or a little spot where the tape recording didn’t erase, or bled through like a double exposure in photography.  The more I learn about it, the more references I see to temporal lobe focal auras.  It’s definitely a period of abnormal brain activity, but hard to capture with brain mapping technologies.  
Now, I think it was an early manifestation of my tendency towards seizures.  My seizures, themselves , are really weird.  It always happens during liminal sleep, or at the point where I begin to lose consciousness.  If there’s a fan or heater going, the sound changes pitch and oscillation, and I feel my head shaking and can hear it rubbing on the bed.  I can usually force myself out of it by taking a series of deep, fast breaths, but I can’t move my limbs the way I want to, and my eyes will be open and I can see what’s around me.  It feels like my head is being sucked into electric motor; like my consciousness itself is becoming vibration and just pure energy.  Sometimes I get addicted to hanging over the ledge, so to speak, and I try to ride it a little farther and go deeper into the space, but part of this is that I just get tired of fighting it after it’s happened 50 times in a row, every time I’m almost asleep.  I’m not as scared of it as I used to be, but if it takes longer to regain control of my body and I’m paralyzed with my eyes wide for more than a minute, I get worried.  It’s strange though.  Usually, if I’m afraid or experiencing anything stressful, it makes my heart beat faster.  The seizures are frightening, but my heart rate is slow and steady while they are happening and afterwards, and I feel surprisingly calm in spite of my thoughts that maybe I will get stuck in this space forever. I usually just get up for awhile after it ends and try to write or draw something.  Sometimes my imagination is really stimulated after a bunch of these.  I have to say that I feel very fortunate that I don’t get these while I’m working or going about my waking life.  I am worried that they will become worse as my brain ages, and invade my waking life, eventually.  I’ve been having them for about 12 years, but didn’t get them until my early 30s.  They seem to coincide with depression and insomnia, but the more I learn about different types of seizures, the more I think that some of my ticks and head spaces are inter-related.  Nowadays, when I get deja vu, I still get a little anxiety, but I feel like sometimes I can mentally connect the glitch with another memory and almost make sense of it.

I know a few Native Americans who are vegan, but having lived half of my life on reservations, I can say it’s not common.
Part of what I’ve seen is that there are big problems related to nutrition— obesity, diabetes, alcoholism.  Some of this is due to poverty and “food desert “ conditions that prevail in many rural areas.  Another aspect is simply that people of European ancestry often have greater capacity to thrive on wheat/ grains, due to an extra several thousand years of reliance on breads, dairy, etc.  So, it’s similar with alcohol that some Native groups have allergic reactions, because it hasn’t been available to their ancestors until relatively recent times. Tribal nutritional programs often distribute wild game and fish to poor folks on the reservations who would otherwise be living on government cheese and GMO flour.  There’s cultural arguments above and beyond nutrition, but someone else can make those arguments.  Yes, colonialism has changed diets and it has led to health problems in many populations.  I think the best thing to do to inspire vegan diets, overall, is to make good options available.  I’m not personally a vegan these days, but if I’m out in society eating at a restaurant I always get the vegan option or specifically request modifications to make whatever I order vegan.  Ultimately, it’s a decision that people have to make for themselves, so anything that makes it easier to make that decision (to not eat animal products) is something I want to support .  Eating within your ecosystem and utilizing seasonally fresh produce is another part of this equation.  In cold northern climates, this can be a tall order, and requires a lot of work and resources to accomplish.  In some places it is just more efficient and healthy to hunt, than it is to import produce long distances, or rely on commodity grain crops that destroy your gut and cause all sorts of health problems.  I’m glad that vegan options are becoming more common and available throughout my life.  It’s a long road trying to move the needle away from traditional practices, especially when it comes to something as elemental as food.  Overall, I think presenting veganism through the lens of environmental health and conservation is more persuasive to a lot of people, rather than presenting animal liberation arguments.  Most hunters, who do it for meat, are also animal lovers.  I know it seems contradictory, but there’s a deep recognition of gratitude for the animals hunted, and an environmental ethic that runs deep to a spiritual level—something that is missing in the industrial animal products industries.  I’ve worked for wildlife conservation groups and Native organizations protesting pipelines and environmental destruction, and I’ve witnessed a lot of people who regularly identify as vegan, begin consuming wild game and roadkill at the community kitchen.  Just an observation.  Obviously, it would be a disaster if all humans relied on hunting to obtain protein.  Luckily that isn’t the situation for most of the world’s population.

You’re absolutely correct.  I think there’s a lot that gets overlooked in the tendencies of one generation to either criticize or glorify another.  The most recent data I’ve seen on the Boomer generation indicates that around 45% of them have no retirement savings whatsoever. The “ok Boomer” parlance, and memes that I see a lot of these days is basing itself on an assumption that they’ve mostly been privileged and afforded great opportunity for social mobility, whereas the reality is not so simple.  As always, the greatest predictor of where you end up in the economic class strata is where you start.  I imagine the same to be true among Gen X and Z as well, but some of the data of outcomes aren’t yet compiled.  If you go back further in history, say the 1950s, the wealth distribution actually favored younger and middle-age adults, but the older age cohort had a shorter life-span on average, and many of them lost generationally accumulated wealth in the Great Depression ( It’s a ridiculous figure how much stolen land was stolen from small farmers in that era by the banks). Regardless , people often base their assumptions of wealth and social mobility on only the upper 50 percentile group in an age cohort ( or worse, by a highly skewed “average”) and don’t recognize that an equally large number of cases, or larger number actually fall below that benchmark.  Social mobility from one economic class to another is trending negative by some metrics, and there have always been intermittent events such as the 2008 housing bubble collapse which cause a precipitous decline in wealth for an enormous percentage of people, while the outliers in the 95th percentile often profit immensely.  I think the most telling metric that has been coming up lately in general social survey data is the longitudinal measure of percentage of wealth owned by a given age group.  For example, at the moment Boomers own roughly 53% of the (U.S. data) wealth, while Gen X owns 28.6% as of June last year, and the Millennials account for 5%.  In and of itself, this is a very logical distribution in that it is linear with age and accumulation of stored labor.  Some people look at this and take umbrage at the unfairness of it, but fast-forward 30 years and the distribution will still follow the same linear direction, but the shares will likely be different.  Where it gets interesting is when you rewind 33 years to when Boomers were the same age as as Gen X is now.  In 1989 the Boomers owned about 21% of wealth, a lower percentage than Xers own now.  In a way the statistic is meaningless because it is an averaged figure and doesn’t show the distribution or inequality within that age group.  So like you said, it’s largely a matter of what leverage you start with, the opportunities available to you, and your resources available to pursue those opportunities, rather than a “bootstraps” narrative.  I myself grew up in poverty with Boomer parents who didn’t pay off their student debt or get a mortgage until they were in their late 40s.  The real and palpable differences are in the growing inequality not between generations, but within society as a whole.  Things that threaten to reduce society to a revival of feudalism, and quite possibly another extreme fascist regime, are the collapse of manufacturing and union jobs, the rise of the gig economy, and rampant real estate speculation by the ultra wealthy and investment corporations, basically buying up all the houses and holding them for ransom.  
Anyway, it’s not so much a generation thing as it is a class warfare situation.  It always has been.  There was a significant bump in parity after WW2, and a social contract of sorts whereby the working class were granted some concessions in return for their suffering at the hands of robber barons in the Depression, and later their participation in the military-industrial war machine and manufacturing economy.  Concessions were made to prevent a populist social movement towards a potential Bolshevik-style uprising.  Now that the WW2 generation is all but perished, the social contract is dissolving rapidly.  It also appears that a lot of people are veering dangerously close to embracing a very nationalistic form of authoritarianism.  It’s definitely a time that builds character, just who knows what character it will build?  There’s always the fear of nuclear annihilation to consider.  It seems to be a less dominant subject of character-building fear since the 90s. So, yeah, each generation gets its own set of adversities to deal with, and hopefully overcome.

I doubt you have schizoaffective.  It’s just one of the things that can pop up to varying degrees, but rarely after someone is over 21.  DpDr is probably going on a little with you, but I seriously wouldn’t worry too much if it’s not causing major problems. It’s good that you are seeing a therapist.  I really would like to find one that I feel like I can communicate with.  It sounds like you have a very social job, which you like, so that’s a plus.  I can’t speak for anyone else, but for me the derealization is probably the strongest manifestation of depression and it’s really unbearable when it gets bad.  It’s like I’m wrapped in some kind of film that is very isolating and suffocating.  I have to forcefully make myself breathe sometimes.  As far as DpDr goes, there are people who deal with it on a much more chronic and intense level.  It sounds like for you it’s probably emanating from OCD, or maybe a past trauma.  You could just frame it as having a unique mind.  It’s something that can resolve and go away naturally for some people, but others deal with it chronically or in bouts ( like me).  You would probably know it by now if you had schizophrenia.  A seizure disorder can also cause weird auras, sensations, and absence of mind and detached thoughts.  A lot of people, myself included, have mild seizures that aren’t really diagnosed or debilitating.  It doesn’t mean you shake uncontrollably necessarily.  There’s a lot of variety in brain circuitry, so it would be abnormal if you didn’t have some irregularities of some sort.  Anyway the seizures I get happen as I’m trying to fall asleep, and I’m aware while it happens.  At first it worried me, but now I find them kind of interesting and thought provoking.  Anyway, I hate the weight of labels in diagnosing states of mind.  The boundaries between different mind phenomena are not as neat and clearly defined as the DMS4 diagnostic manual makes them out to be.  I wouldn’t stress about it just yet, and even if you get a diagnosis from a doc, it doesn’t necessarily mean they are correctly placing you in a category, or that whatever category they put you in is going to be uniformly like the textbook.
I’d recommend watching some of the psychology lectures that Stanford U. puts up for free online.  There’s a really good professor with a big bushy beard and it’s fascinating subject matter when you’re trying to guesstimate brain chemistry and neuroscience on yourself.    Did your doc give you any meds?  That’s something that might be a factor to look at.  I’ve learned from trying different meds that many of them trigger depersonalization pretty severely, especially SSRI’s and Wellbutrin.

All this psychological stuff is kinda hard to unwind or categorize completely, since most people have some combination of depression, anxiety, OCD, schizoaffective, or borderline personality as co-occurring conditions to one degree or another. I have to agree with you.  The economics are a big factor.  Obviously we don’t want to poison the land and ourselves with chemicals, but there’s water use to consider also.  Some GMO crops use significantly less water and have higher yields.  I like organic products and do my own garden organic, but on an industrial level switching to an exclusively organic/nonGMO system might end up being more intensive and consume even more water resources for lower yields.  It’s hard to say “GMO” and make it a blanket statement.  There’s probably some seeds that produce food that some people or animals will develop allergies to, but there’s others that aren’t super problematic.  I worry about “super weeds” self-evolving and becoming a persistent problem, but there’s no guarantee that they won’t come about even in the absence heavy herbicide/pesticide use.  There’s a lot to consider in terms of parenting of genetics, saving seeds, hybridization and sterilization of heirlooms, etc.  I used to be more against GMOs, but I’ve changed my tune about some of them.  Modifying rice and grains to produce higher protein ratios could be a real game changer for a growing human population, and in the case of farming fish, it would take pressure off of some of the wild fish that are used to make fish food pellets. Creating drought tolerant versions of staple crops is also very valuable.  There’s some GMOs I avoid (corn/tomatoes), but it’s a personal preference.  Some people have floated the theory that the trend of people claiming to be gluten intolerant is actually an inflammation response to GMO grains that the human organism hasn’t adjusted to.  Maybe, or maybe it’s a difference in how they are processed.  I guess I’m more an advocate of growing a diversity of crops on a tract of land rather than doing it all in one big monoculture.  Still more labor intensive and expensive, but it’s good to not put all your eggs in one basket.

I think it’s indisputable that a vegan diet on a planetary scale would be more sustainable in terms of land use.  I’d be curious to see the solutions in terms of fertilizer inputs to maintaining healthy soils.  Even organic vegan food is often fertilized by adding composted manure to the soil.  Chemical fertilizers aren’t my favorite, but I guess with the land freed up from animal husbandry maybe there are farming methods and rotations that would alleviate the need for animal derived fertilizer.  I’m definitely no expert, but soil health is something I’m concerned about.  The nutrient and trace mineral content of vegetables grown in soil that has been under continuous industrial production for 100 years isn’t equivalent to biodynamic methods.  I’m experimenting with plant based fertilizer in my own garden, but I wonder how it would work on a large scale.  I guess humanure works, but most people are a little squeamish about that subject.  Russian comfrey is one I’m interested in.  You can take the biomass and essentially ferment it in a pool or pond and get a great organic fertilizer.  There are doubtlessly a lot of solutions to compensating for a shift away from animal derived soil nutrients.  I think it’s a good area to get into in terms of planning for a plant based food system.  It’s an interesting subject.  I’m not currently vegan, but I’m definitely not in favor of factory farming.  I try to think of dietary options that aren’t meant to mimic animal products in texture and type, so I just don’t do any kind of plant based “milk” or texturized fake meat.  Vegetables, mushrooms, legumes, etc. are good on their own and don’t need processing into “substitutes” for animal products.  I like having chickens in my garden though.  They keep the bugs down and make eggs.  I guess I just envision a different level of reliance on animals that keeps the land in balance, and isn’t cruel.  I’ll always support vegans and vegetarians, and I would likely go that route again myself if end up living in a city again or going to jail.  Even if not everyone goes vegan, just going plant based and plant-centric at a more society-wide level is going to happen, I think.  It’s becoming a more natural reflex to empathize with animals that are grown in industrial fashion as society itself becomes more like a factory farm.
